results.summary: This analog block contains a temperature sensor that is one of a group of student designs. The pin list shows only a power-up input and a temperature-dependent oscillator output, and there is no documentation beyond the one-line description. A user would power the block and measure the output frequency, but without a data sheet or schematic the behaviour cannot be verified. The documentation is essentially absent, so the functionality is inferred from the title and pin names.

This analog block is a temperature sensor built by a student group. The pins provide start and power-up controls, an eight-bit parallel temperature output, and a temperature-dependent oscillator output. No documentation is provided beyond the title and pin names, so the exact encoding and accuracy of the eight-bit value are unknown. The design would be used by powering it up, starting a conversion, and reading the digital temperature word, but the lack of documentation makes its capabilities difficult to assess.

The design is an analog temperature-to-frequency sensor that uses a bandgap circuit to produce a PTAT current and CTAT voltage, which a relaxation oscillator converts to a frequency. It is used by powering the analog core and measuring the frequency on the output pin with a counter or logic analyzer; sweeping the ambient temperature allows calibration. No external hardware is needed beyond a frequency measurement tool, and the design was created to meet a specified temperature-sensor brief. Notable details include a non-linear frequency-versus-temperature curve that requires compensation and silicon measurements are not reported in the documentation.

The LSC-1 Micro is a SystemVerilog arithmetic kernel implementing XOR, GF(2^128) multiplication, and SET operations over a byte-wide ready/valid interface. It accepts an opcode followed by a fixed-size payload and returns a 16-byte response, with support for request and response stalls and a fault indication for unsupported opcodes. The core requires a 25 MHz clock, active-low reset, and chip enable, and is intended to be driven by a host controller or microcontroller; no external memory or packet framing is included. The design is a reduced sub-core of the larger LSC-1 and does not include BLAKE3 or other full-system features, and testing is performed by host-side arithmetic comparison.

This design is a hardware accelerator for the Simon block cipher in its 32/64 configuration, with an SPI slave interface that allows a master to load a key and data block, select encryption or decryption, and read the result. It also includes a variable-frequency ring oscillator and an analog multiplexer for measurement, with an analog output pin intended for oscilloscope monitoring. Testing can be done via an RP2350B microcontroller using SPI and GPIO control, and an oscilloscope with low-capacitance probes is required for the analog output. The design is a second version that adds the oscillator and measurement capability, though detailed silicon results are not included.

The design implements a Bloom filter for probabilistic set membership testing using a 64-bit array and two XOR-fold hash functions on 8-bit inputs. It supports insert and query operations through a simple strobe interface, with a VALID signal indicating completion and a RESULT output for queries; debug outputs expose the computed hash indices. It requires no external hardware beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout demo board, and the documentation explains the operation sequence and timing. The design guarantees no false negatives and may produce false positives, as expected for a Bloom filter.

This project is a digital simulation of two qubits and an entangled pair, imitating quantum behaviour with registers, comparators, and three maximal-length LFSRs for probabilistic collapse. It is controlled by four input switches for initial states, Hadamard gate application, and measurement, with four LED outputs displaying the results. The design was prototyped in Wokwi and uses a 100 Hz clock, making it suitable for educational demonstrations. It does not perform real quantum computation and the randomness is a simplified stand-in based on LFSRs.

This analog block implements an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter with a 3.3 V output achieved through level-shifting drivers. It can be driven externally via the digital input pins or by an internal digital sine waveform generator, with control pins for loading and an external data input. An oscilloscope is required to measure the analog output voltage on the dedicated analog pin. The design is straightforward and no detailed performance specifications are provided.

This design is a neural network inference engine with four signed 4-bit MAC lanes that compute four dot products per job with 20-bit accumulation. It uses an acknowledged byte interface to receive commands and data from a host and to stream back twelve result bytes, with support for optional biases. The host is responsible for activation functions, requantization, and multilayer scheduling, as the core returns raw signed sums; a standalone ReLU block exists but is not connected. The design targets a 50 MHz clock pending SKY130 timing verification and requires a host with memory for images and weights, plus a Tiny Tapeout demo board or compatible host.

This Verilog design implements a streaming ML-KEM ciphertext codec and Fujisaki-Okamoto integrity checker supporting all three standard parameter sets (512, 768, 1024). It has two phases: decompression of bit-packed coefficients and auxiliary-reference verification where a recompressed coefficient is compared against the ciphertext, accumulating a sticky mismatch flag. The design is controlled via start, phase, and parameter bits, and communicates over the standard Tiny Tapeout pins with no external hardware required. Notable features include a divider-free bit-serial design, a parameter mismatch fault indication, and a cocotb test suite that exercises all parameter sets and tamper injection.
